title: Switch it

brief.story: The club's door sign needs its LED switched by a microcontroller pin, but a pin can only give a trickle of current. The button stands in for the pin here. Q1, a BC547, is in, with the LED and its resistor on its collector. Nothing joins the button to Q1's base yet.
brief.goal: Join the button to Q1's base through a resistor, so LED1 lights at 10–25 mA while the button is held, with no more than 2 mA going into the base.

datasheet.title: Q1 · BC547 (NPN)
rows: E · B · C, left to right

hints: The button's far leg is in column 7. Q1's base is its middle leg, in column 11. A resistor goes from one column to the other.
The base current is about (9 V − 0.7 V) ÷ R. Under 2 mA means R over about 4.2 kΩ.
Try 10 kΩ: 0.83 mA into the base, and up to 200 × that could flow in the collector: plenty to switch the LED fully on.

spec.explain: LED1's current comes through Q1, and Q1 only lets through what its base current allows: about 200 × I_B. Too big a base resistor starves it.

spec.label: Base current under 2 mA
spec.explain: A pin can only give a few mA. The base resistor sets the base current: (9 V − 0.7 V) ÷ R.

debrief: A trickle into the base switched fourteen times as much through the LED. That's what every Arduino project with a motor, relay or LED strip does: a pin drives a base (or a MOSFET's gate) through a resistor, and the transistor does the heavy lifting.
